meta_title: Rapture & Second Coming Q&A — What does the Bible say about the pretribulation rapture? | Bible Insight
meta_desc: A careful, step-by-step look at the pretribulation rapture from the text of Scripture: the meaning of the word, ten lines of biblical evidence, the Jewish wedding custom and the parable of the ten virgins, Israel and the church, traces in church history, seventeen common objections with answers, and how to discern if a figure like the Antichrist appears without a rapture. With theological notes and a checked bibliography.
title: Rapture & Second Coming Q&A
subtitle: What does the Bible say about the pretribulation rapture?
lead: This section was not written to calculate dates or to frighten anyone. It was written to examine from Scripture the "blessed hope" the Bible promises, and to help us live watchfully today. Bible Insight teaches the pretribulation rapture as the view that best fits the biblical text. We also gladly honor believers who hold other views as brothers and sisters waiting for the same Lord.
updated: Written November 2026 · Bible Insight editorial team

sections.h: 1. Four Things to Make Clear First

body.note: **This is not about dates.** Nothing in this section calculates the day, the year or the season of the rapture or the Second Coming. No one knows that day and hour (Matt. 24:36).

**This is not a matter of salvation.** Whether the rapture comes before, in the middle of, or after the Tribulation is a difference of interpretation that has long been discussed within historic orthodox faith. Which view you hold does not decide your salvation.

**We respect every view.** The faithful believers before us who held premillennialism, amillennialism or postmillennialism were all waiting for the same Lord. This section only explains why the pretribulation rapture is persuasive. It does not attack other views.

**We keep pictures and proof apart.** Stories such as those of Noah, Lot and Enoch, or the wedding customs, are pictures (types) that help us understand the Bible. We do not build doctrine on pictures alone. We read them together with the direct words of Scripture.

sections.h: 2. What Is the Rapture? — Starting with the Word

body.p: The rapture is the event in which the Lord descends into the air: believers who have died in Christ are raised first, and believers who are still alive are changed in body and caught up together with them to meet the Lord.

The Greek word translated "caught up" is **harpazō (ἁρπάζω)**. It means to snatch away suddenly and by force.[^1] Its meaning becomes even clearer when we see how the same word is used elsewhere in the New Testament.

ul: The Spirit of the Lord **caught away** Philip (Acts 8:39) — moved him in an instant to another place
Paul was **caught up** to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2, 4) — taken up into heaven
The chief captain had his soldiers **take him by force** from among the crowd (Acts 23:10) — rescued by force from danger
Some are saved by **pulling them out of the fire** (Jude 1:23) — rescued just before destruction
The child born to the woman was **caught up** unto God and to His throne (Rev. 12:5) — out of the enemy's hand and into heaven

body.p: Around the fourth century the Bible was translated into Latin (the Vulgate), and it rendered these words in 1 Thess. 4:17 as rapiemur ("we shall be caught up"). The root is rapio ("to snatch"), and from it comes the English word "rapture." It is a theological term that simply names what this verse describes: being lifted up and carried away.
So the rapture is not people escaping on their own. It is a **rescue**: the Lord takes hold of His people in an instant and lifts them up. The word itself carries that picture.

Paul calls this a "mystery," that is, a new revelation that was not made known in the Old Testament. It is the promise that there will be a generation who are changed in an instant without passing through death.

sections.h: 3. A Map of the Views — the Timing of the Rapture and the Millennium

body.p: Most Bible-believing scholars agree that there will be a rapture. Where they differ is **when**. The reference point is Daniel's seventieth week, the seven-year Tribulation that comes just before the Lord returns to the earth.[^2]

body.p: Views also differ on how to read the "thousand years" of Revelation 20. **Premillennialism** holds that the Lord comes again before the millennial kingdom. It has two forms, historic premillennialism and dispensational premillennialism. **Amillennialism** reads the "thousand years" as a symbol of the church age, from the Ascension to the Second Coming. **Postmillennialism** holds that the Lord comes after the gospel has spread widely throughout the world. All of these are interpretations that faithful believers have held throughout church history.

**Dispensationalism** is a way of reading the Bible that was organized into a system in the nineteenth century. It reads the history of the Bible in several eras (dispensations), distinguishes Israel from the church, and explains the last days in this order: pretribulation rapture → seven-year Tribulation → Second Coming → Millennium. Dispensationalism is one of the systems of interpretation that have long been discussed within the orthodox church. It is not a heresy that denies the faith confessed in the Apostles' Creed. It is true that some have borrowed its name to set dates, to make people follow a particular leader, or to make them give away their property. Such deviations have nothing to do with this interpretation.

body.note: All four views are differences of interpretation within historic orthodox faith. The timing of the rapture is not a condition of salvation.[^3]

sections.h: 4. Ten Lines of Biblical Evidence for the Pretribulation Rapture

body.h3: ① He may come at any time — imminence

body.p: The believers of the New Testament did not say that the Lord would come only after certain signs had all been fulfilled. They waited for a Lord who might come that very day. This is called **imminence**. If the rapture happened at the end of the seven-year Tribulation, people could count the days from the day the Tribulation began, that is, from the day the covenant of Daniel 9:27 is confirmed. A rapture that waits for no sign best keeps the words "in such an hour as ye think not" and "of that day and hour knoweth no man."[^4]

body.h3: ② He delivers us from wrath

body.p: In Revelation, already at the opening of the sixth seal the people of the earth cry out, "the great day of his wrath is come" (Rev. 6:16–17), and with the seven last plagues "is filled up the wrath of God" (Rev. 15:1). If the Tribulation is thus a time when God's wrath comes upon the earth, the promise that believers are not appointed to that wrath fits best with being taken out of that period.

body.h3: ③ He keeps us from the "hour" of trial

body.p: "Keep thee from" translates the Greek **tēreō ek (τηρέω ἐκ)**, "to keep out of." The Lord does not say He will protect the church in the middle of the trial. He says He will keep it from the very "hour" (hōra) of trial that will come upon the whole world.[^5] The objections to this verse and our answers are covered in detail in Objection 5 below.

body.h3: ④ He rescues first, then judges — Noah, Lot and Enoch

body.p: The Lord compared the day of the Son of man to the days of Noah and the days of Lot. Both stories follow the same order. God's people are first moved to a safe place, and then judgment falls. The angel at Sodom said, "I cannot do anything till thou be come thither." The judgment was already decided, but it could not begin until the righteous man had gone out.

Long before Noah went into the ark, Enoch was taken to God without seeing death. Many interpreters have read Enoch, taken away before the Flood, as a picture of the church caught up in the rapture, and Noah, preserved through the Flood, as a picture of the remnant kept through the Tribulation. This is a type, so it is not proof in itself. But it points in the same direction as the direct words of Scripture above.

The Greek word translated "escape" is **ekpheugō (ἐκφεύγω)**, which means to get out of, to get away from.[^6] The Lord did not only tell us to endure all these things. He told us to pray that we may "escape" them, and He ended with "to stand before the Son of man." This is not a picture of passing through the troubles on earth. It is a picture of being brought before the Lord.

body.h3: ⑥ The Bridegroom comes at midnight — the parable of the ten virgins

ul: The bridegroom comes **without warning**, at midnight, when the wait has grown long and everyone has fallen asleep.
Those who are ready go in **with him** to the marriage. The bridegroom comes in order to take the bride.
Then **the door is shut.** Some people are left outside.
The point of the parable is not calculation but **readiness**: "Watch therefore."

body.h3: ⑦ The Bridegroom takes the bride to the Father's house — the Jewish wedding custom

body.p: The New Testament calls the church the bride of Christ (2 Cor. 11:2; Eph. 5:25–27; Rev. 19:7). The order of the Jewish wedding custom, as it is known from the time of Jesus, is remarkably like the way the Lord deals with His church.[^7]

head: Wedding custom
Christ and the church
rows: ① Betrothal — the bridegroom pays a price and they share a cup of the covenant. From this point they are legally husband and wife.
Believers "bought with a price" (1 Cor. 6:20); "This cup is the new testament in my blood" (Luke 22:20)
② The bridegroom goes back to his father's house and prepares a place to live with his bride.
"I go to prepare a place for you" (John 14:2)
③ The father decides the day the bridegroom goes to fetch her.
That day and hour only the Father knows (Matt. 24:36)
④ The bride does not know when he will come, so she stays ready and pure as she waits.
"Every man that hath this hope in him purifieth himself" (1 John 3:3)
⑤ The bridegroom comes suddenly at night, with a shout and the sound of a trumpet.
"At midnight there was a cry made" (Matt. 25:6); "with a shout ... and with the trump of God" (1 Thess. 4:16)
⑥ The bridegroom does not stay at the bride's house. He takes the bride away with him.
"I will come again, and receive you unto myself" (John 14:3); "to meet the Lord in the air" (1 Thess. 4:17)
⑦ The wedding feast is held for seven days at the father's house.
"Fulfil her week" (Gen. 29:27); "the seven days of the feast" (Judg. 14:12); "the marriage of the Lamb" (Rev. 19:7)
⑧ After the feast, the bridegroom and the bride appear together.
"The armies which were in heaven followed him" (Rev. 19:14); "then shall ye also appear with him in glory" (Col. 3:4)

body.p: Seen through this picture, Christ the Bridegroom first comes and takes His bride, the church, to the Father's house (the rapture). While the seven-year Tribulation passes on earth, the marriage supper of the Lamb is held in heaven. After that, He appears in glory together with His bride (the Second Coming).

It is also meaningful that Jesus' first sign took place at a wedding feast on "the third day." The ruler of the feast said, "thou hast kept the good wine until now" (John 2:1, 10). The Lord's ministry began at a wedding feast, and it will be completed at the marriage supper of the Lamb. The best has been kept for last.

body.note: Many interpreters and preachers have described this custom on the basis of ancient Jewish writings, and the details may have differed by region and period. It is a beautiful picture for understanding the Bible, but it is not proof of doctrine in itself. Please read it together with the direct words of Scripture above.

body.p: If these are merged into one event, the texts collide. Read as two stages with the Tribulation between them, each text finds its place.

body.h3: ⑨ The flow of Revelation — the word "church" disappears

body.p: In Revelation 1–3 the word "church" (ekklēsia) appears nineteen times. But in chapters 4–18, which describe the Tribulation on earth, the church on earth is not mentioned even once. Then the word appears again in 22:16.[^8]

Chapter 4 begins with the call "Come up hither." And already around the throne in heaven sit twenty-four elders, clothed in white and wearing crowns of gold (Rev. 4:4). Many interpreters read them as representatives of the church, already taken up to heaven and rewarded.

body.h3: ⑩ When the restrainer is taken out of the way

body.p: Before the man of sin is revealed, the one who now restrains him must first be taken out of the way. The pretribulation view understands this restrainer as the work of the Holy Spirit, who dwells in the church and holds back the lawlessness of the world. It reads that this restraint is lifted when the church is caught up.[^9]

sections.h: 5. Israel and the Church — Whom Is the Final Week For?

body.p: **Replacement theology** is the view that the church has replaced Israel. Because Israel rejected Christ, it says, the promises God gave to Israel in the Old Testament have now all passed spiritually to the church, and God's plan for Israel as a people is finished. It is also a view that has been widely held for a long time in church history.

Paul says that God has not cast away His people, and that His calling is "without repentance." Daniel's seventy weeks are determined "upon thy people and upon thy holy city," and Jeremiah calls the final trouble "the time of Jacob’s trouble." So the pretribulation view does not see the seven-year Tribulation as a time for refining the church. It sees it as the time when God calls Israel back to Himself and judges the world. When the church and Israel are read as distinct, the order in which the church, the bride, is taken away beforehand follows naturally. On the other hand, if the church has completely replaced Israel, then the believers who go through the Tribulation must also be the church, and the reading leans toward placing the rapture after the Tribulation.

body.note: This distinction does not mean that there are two ways of salvation. Jews and Gentiles alike are saved only in Christ, only by faith. This article also neither supports nor criticizes the politics or wars of any nation today, and it does not condemn brothers and sisters who hold replacement theology.

body.p: The pretribulation rapture was organized into a system in the nineteenth century. But the seeds of the idea can be seen much earlier.

ul: **The early church's eager waiting** — The Didache, a church document from the early second century, urges believers in chapter 16 to keep watch, because they do not know the hour when the Lord is coming. The early church did not push the Lord's coming off into the distant future.[^10]

**Hippolytus (early third century)** — He saw Daniel's final "week" as a period that remains at the end of the world, after the gospel has been preached to the whole world. He did not teach a rapture. But this is a trace showing that the reading which sets the final week apart and places it in the future existed from a very early time.[^11]

**An old sermon handed down under the name of Ephraem (4th–7th century)** — It contains a sentence to the effect that all the saints and the elect are gathered and taken to the Lord before the coming tribulation, so that they do not see the confusion that will overwhelm the world. Scholars discuss how this sentence should be read, so we present it as a "source under discussion."[^12]

**After the Reformation** — Preachers and commentators who read the Bible literally and took prophecy seriously gradually set forth the idea of distinguishing the rapture from the Second Coming. A 1788 work by the American Baptist minister Morgan Edwards is a leading example. The idea was then organized into a system in the nineteenth century.[^13]

body.p: What matters is not so much when an interpretation was organized into a system, but whether it comes from the biblical text. The Trinity and justification by faith were also formally stated at particular times, but their roots are in Scripture.

In fairness, we set the questions raised by other views side by side with the answers of the pretribulation view. The brothers and sisters who ask these questions are waiting for the same Lord. Being awake on that day matters more than who turns out to be right.

qa.q: 1. In Matthew 24:31 the elect are gathered "after the tribulation of those days." Doesn't that put the rapture after the Tribulation?

a.p: The Olivet Discourse is spoken first of all with "them which be in Judaea" (24:16) and "the sabbath day" (24:20) in view. Here the ones who gather the elect from the four winds are **the angels**. It is the scene in which God fulfills His promise to gather scattered Israel with the sound of a great trumpet (Isa. 27:13; Deut. 30:4). The rapture is different. The Lord **Himself** comes down, and believers meet Him **in the air** (1 Thess. 4:16–17). The Second Coming is a day that all the tribes of the earth will see and mourn (Matt. 24:30), but the rapture happens in the twinkling of an eye and brings "comfort" to believers (1 Thess. 4:18). These "elect" are most naturally read as those who come to faith during the Tribulation after the rapture, together with the remnant of Israel whom God gathers again.[^14]

qa.q: 2. Isn't "the last trump" (1 Cor. 15:52) the seventh trumpet of Revelation (Rev. 11:15)? Both passages speak of a "mystery."

ul: **They were written at different times.** First Corinthians was written about forty years before Revelation. The Corinthian believers could not have known about a seventh trumpet that had not yet been written down. So Paul's "last trump" is most naturally read as something he had already taught them: "the trump of God" that gathers the saints (1 Thess. 4:16).

**Who blows it, and what follows, are different.** The trumpet of the rapture is "the trump of God," and it ends with "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thess. 4:18). The seven trumpets of Revelation are trumpets of judgment blown by angels, and even after the seventh trumpet come "the third woe" (Rev. 11:14) and the seven bowl judgments.

**"Mystery" is not the name of a single event.** The New Testament word "mystery" (mystērion) appears more than twenty times. It is used for many different things: the blindness of Israel (Rom. 11:25), the church (Eph. 3:3–6), Christ and the church (Eph. 5:32), the seven stars (Rev. 1:20) and Babylon the great (Rev. 17:5). What is more, the mystery in Rev. 10:7 was already known, "as he hath declared to his servants the prophets," while the mystery Paul speaks of is one "which in other ages was not made known unto the sons of men" (Eph. 3:5).

**If "last" means last in a sequence,** there is also a trumpet after the seventh: the "great sound of a trumpet" at the Second Coming (Matt. 24:31). The single word "last" cannot tie the two trumpets together as one.

qa.q: 3. Doesn't 2 Thessalonians 2:3 say that the falling away and the man of sin must come "first" before that day comes?

a.p: The "day" Paul speaks of is not the rapture but the Day of the Lord, the day of judgment. The Thessalonian believers had been shaken by word that this day had already come (2 Thess. 2:2). Paul corrects them: that day has not yet come, and when it comes, the falling away and the revealing of the man of sin will go with it. He also says that the man of sin is revealed only after "he who now letteth" is taken out of the way (2:6–8).

It is also worth noticing **why** they were shaken. If they had been taught that they would be caught up at the end of the Tribulation, the news that the Day of the Lord had come would actually have been welcome news. The natural explanation is that they were afraid because they had been taught the hope of being caught up before that day, and thought they had missed that gathering.[^15]

qa.q: 4. Aren't the people in white robes who "came out of great tribulation" (Rev. 7:14) the church?

a.p: In the original, "came out" is in the present tense: "those who are coming out." It pictures people who turn to the Lord and are martyred throughout the Tribulation, arriving in heaven one after another. The church is already before the throne in chapter 4, as the twenty-four elders clothed in white and wearing crowns of gold (Rev. 4:4). That is why the elder asks John, "What are these which are arrayed in white robes? and whence came they?" (7:13). If they were the church, there would be no reason to ask. This multitude is evidence of grace: even after the rapture, God does not shut the door of salvation.

qa.q: 5. Doesn't "keep" (tēreō ek) in Rev. 3:10 mean "to preserve inside," as in John 17:15?

a.p: John 17 uses two different kinds of "keeping." In verse 11, "keep through thine own name" is **tēreō en** (to keep within). In verse 15, "keep them from the evil" is **tēreō ek** (to keep out of). Verse 15 is also a prayer that the disciples be kept **outside** the grip of the evil one, not a prayer that they hold out while inside it. Rev. 3:10 uses ek, and what follows is not simply the trial but the **hour** (hōra) of trial, that is, a period of time.

Also, that hour is the hour "to try them that dwell upon the earth." In Revelation, "them that dwell upon the earth" is a name for those who oppose God (6:10; 13:8; 17:8). If the verse meant "preserved inside," it would not fit the passages that say many believers will be martyred during the Tribulation (6:9–11; 13:7). And if it meant only that God keeps their souls, that is already promised to every believer (John 10:28), so there would be no reason to promise it as a special reward to the church in Philadelphia alone.

To be fair, some scholars read ek as "coming out from within." Even read that way, the word alone does not decide whether that coming out happens before the hour of trial or at its end. So it must be read together with the context above.[^5]

qa.q: 6. Doesn't the wrath begin only with the sixth seal, at the end of the Tribulation? Until then, aren't believers protected in the middle of it, as Israel was in Goshen?

a.p: The seals in Revelation are opened by **the Lamb Himself**, starting with the first one (Rev. 6:1). By the fourth seal, a fourth of the earth has already been killed (6:8). This is not human persecution; it is judgment that comes from the Lamb's hand. So when the kings of the earth cry out at the sixth seal, "the great day of his wrath is come" (6:17), it reads not as the moment the wrath begins, but as the moment they recognize the wrath that has already come. Examples of God keeping His people in the midst of trouble, such as Goshen (Exod. 8:22), the lions' den and the fiery furnace, are precious. But Rev. 7:3 and 9:4 say clearly that the servants who are sealed are from the twelve tribes of Israel (7:4–8). The pretribulation view says just as clearly that there will be believers in the Tribulation. They are the believers who turn to the Lord after the rapture.

qa.q: 7. Jesus said, "when ye shall see all these things, know that it is near" (Matt. 24:33), and "those days shall be shortened" (24:22). So even if the rapture is at the end of the Tribulation, no one could count the days, could they?

a.p: "Shall be shortened" does not mean that God keeps the day hidden. It means that He sets a limit to that period and cuts it off. In fact, Scripture gives exact numbers: 1,260 days and forty-two months (Rev. 11:2–3; 12:6; 13:5), and 1,290 days (Dan. 12:11). Counting from the day the abomination of desolation stands in the holy place (Matt. 24:15), the day can be worked out. Yet the Lord said, "in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh" (Matt. 24:44), and "ye know neither the day nor the hour" (25:13). "Know that it is near" was spoken to the Tribulation saints who await the Second Coming. To the church He gave the imminent hope that He may come even today.

qa.q: 8. There is only one Second Coming. Isn't it unbiblical to say that He comes twice, once to the air and once to the earth? I've heard that "meet" is a word for going out to welcome a king and then coming back down to the earth with him.

a.p: The Second Coming is one event that takes place in two stages. The First Coming, too, held His birth, ministry, cross and resurrection within a single "coming." In the synagogue at Nazareth, Jesus read from Isa. 61:2, stopped at "the acceptable year of the Lord," and left "the day of vengeance of our God" for later (Luke 4:19). The Second Coming likewise has a scene in the air, when He comes **for** His saints (1 Thess. 4:17), and a scene on earth, when He comes **with** His saints (Zech. 14:5; Jude 1:14; Col. 3:4).

It is true that the Greek word translated "meet," **apantēsis**, was used in the ancient world for going out of a city to welcome an important official. But there is also research showing that the word itself does not decide which way people go after the meeting.[^16] Jesus said He would prepare a place "In my Father’s house" and "receive you unto myself; that where I am, there ye may be also" (John 14:2–3). The saints are in the Father's house, and then they come down following the Lord, clothed in white (Rev. 19:14).

qa.q: 9. In the Flood, those who were taken were the ones destroyed, and Noah was left. So isn't being taken a curse and being left a blessing?

a.p: In Matt. 24:40, "taken" is the Greek **paralambanō**, the very word Jesus used in "receive you unto myself" (John 14:3). But the word for the flood that "took them all away" (24:39) is an entirely different word, **airō**.[^17] Being taken is the Lord receiving His own; being left is judgment.

The point of the Lord's comparison with the days of Noah was ordinary daily life: people were "eating and drinking, marrying and giving in marriage" (Matt. 24:38). At the end of the Tribulation, a fourth of the earth (Rev. 6:8) and then a third of men (9:15) would already have died. Could the world still be marrying and giving in marriage as usual then? A picture of something sudden breaking into everyday life fits better before the Tribulation.

qa.q: 10. Noah was preserved through the Flood. Isn't the church, too, preserved through the Tribulation?

a.p: If Noah is a picture, so is Lot, and Lot's case is even clearer. The angel said, "I cannot do anything till thou be come thither" (Gen. 19:22), and "the same day that Lot went out of Sodom it rained fire and brimstone" (Luke 17:29). There is also Enoch, taken away before the Flood (Heb. 11:5). What these types show is not the length of the gap but the order: the righteous must go out first, and then judgment begins. Noah can be read as a picture of the remnant kept through the Tribulation, that is, those who turn to the Lord after the rapture.

qa.q: 11. "The first resurrection" in Rev. 20:5 comes after the Tribulation. Doesn't that mean there is no resurrection (rapture) before it?

a.p: "The first resurrection" refers not to a single date but to a **kind** of resurrection: "the resurrection of life" (John 5:29), "the resurrection of the just" (Luke 14:14). Scripture says this resurrection happens to "every man in his own order": Christ the firstfruits, then those who are Christ's at His coming, and then the martyrs of the Tribulation, who did not worship the beast and were beheaded (Rev. 20:4). Rev. 20:4–5 is the scene in which the first resurrection is **completed**. It does not say that there was no resurrection before it. The proof is that the resurrection of Christ, the firstfruits of the first resurrection, already took place two thousand years ago.[^18]

qa.q: 12. Don't believers go through the Tribulation and then get caught up at the end, together with the Second Coming?

a.p: Scripture distinguishes the two scenes (see the comparison table in ⑧ above). In Revelation, too, after "Come up hither" in chapter 4, the church does not appear on earth all the way through chapter 18. Then in chapter 19 the bride, made ready in heaven, comes down with the Lord (Rev. 19:7–14). If the rapture is at the end of the Tribulation, three questions remain for us to think about together.

ul: **The day no one knows.** Counting 1,260 days (Rev. 12:6) or 1,290 days (Dan. 12:11) from the abomination of desolation (Matt. 24:15) would give the day. Yet the Lord said, "ye know neither the day nor the hour" (Matt. 25:13).

**Those who enter the Millennium.** If at the end of the Tribulation all believers are caught up and given glorified bodies, and the wicked are judged, it is hard to explain where certain people come from: those who enter the Millennium in mortal bodies and have children (Isa. 65:20), and the nations who will be deceived again after the thousand years (Rev. 20:7–8).
**The saints who come with Him.** The saints who follow the Lord from heaven at the Second Coming, clothed in fine linen (Rev. 19:8, 14), must already be in heaven before that (Col. 3:4; Zech. 14:5).

qa.q: 13. I've heard that the pretribulation rapture was invented by the sixteenth-century Jesuits (Catholic) to turn aside the interpretation that identified them with the harlot of Revelation. Is that true?

a.p: Let us first set out the historical facts. What the Jesuit theologian Ribera taught in the late sixteenth century was the interpretation that the Antichrist is one person who will come in the distant future, that is, **futurism**. It has nothing to do with the timing of the rapture, and most of those who believe in a posttribulation rapture hold this futurism too. The claim that "the Jesuit priest Lacunza wrote at the pope's command" is also untrue. In fact, the book on the Second Coming by Lacunza (1731–1801) was placed on the Catholic Church's Index of Forbidden Books in September 1824. A book written at the Vatican's command would hardly have been banned.[^19] As for the claim that he was a "secret Rosicrucian agent," no historical source has been found to support it. Moreover, official Catholic teaching does not accept the idea of an earthly millennial kingdom at all, so it would have had no reason to invent a rapture doctrine.[^20]

The man who translated Lacunza's book into English (1827) was Edward Irving. That is why people often draw the line "Lacunza → Irving → Darby." But Irving himself did not teach a pretribulation rapture. And there are both claims that Darby borrowed the idea from Irving's circle and studies that refute those claims.[^21] Above all, the standard of truth is not "Where did it come from?" but "What does the Bible say?" (Acts 17:11).

qa.q: 14. Isn't this a doctrine that came from nineteenth-century dreams and visions? I've heard that the word "rapture" did not even exist until the late eighteenth century.

a.p: The basis is not dreams but the Word: "Jesus, which delivered us from the wrath to come" (1 Thess. 1:10); "God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation" (1 Thess. 5:9); "I also will keep thee from the hour of temptation" (Rev. 3:10); "I will come again, and receive you unto myself" (John 14:3). The claim that it began with the vision of a woman in Scotland in 1830 is also judged by scholars to have weak support.[^22]

The word "rapture" comes from the fourth-century Latin Bible, which rendered 1 Thess. 4:17 with rapiemur. So its root has been in the Bible for more than 1,600 years. If we judged by when a word was first used, even the word "Trinity" was not used before the late second century.[^23] The standard is not the age of a word but the Word of God.

qa.q: 15. If it was organized into a system in the nineteenth century, isn't it a late idea, and therefore a wrong one?

a.p: It is true that it was organized into a system in the nineteenth century. But the text "caught up" (1 Thess. 4:17) and the teaching to stay awake at all times belonged to the church from the beginning (Section 6). Being organized late does not make an idea wrong.

The restoration of Israel is a good example. Ezekiel 36–37 and Isaiah 11:11–12 say that the scattered people will be gathered back to their land. For most of church history, the mainstream interpretation explained these words only as figures of the church, and only a minority believed them literally. Nineteenth-century interpreters who read prophecy literally expected the scattered people to actually return to the land. When Israel became a nation again in 1948, it became clear that their reading had been faithful to the text. Yet the whole people have not yet turned to the Lord. In Ezekiel 37, too, the bones come together first, and the breath enters them later (Ezek. 37:7–10). This is not a judgment about today's international politics or conflicts. It is about the way we read the Word.
An old majority interpretation is not always right. The standard is always Scripture (Acts 17:11).

qa.q: 16. Isn't the pretribulation rapture a dangerous doctrine that leaves believers unprepared? Isn't it a faith that just wants to avoid suffering?

a.p: Those who are caught up are not the people who got the timing right. They are the people who are **in Christ** (1 Thess. 4:16–17). The timing is not a condition of salvation. Christians suffer hardship and persecution even now (John 16:33). What the pretribulation rapture says is not that there will be no suffering. It says that God will rescue His bride from the final period when His **wrath** is poured out (Rev. 6:16–17).

The imminent hope that He may come even today actually keeps us awake now. It is rather the thought "there are still seven years left" that comes close to the danger of the servant who said, "My lord delayeth his coming" (Matt. 24:48). Scripture tells us to hold this hope firmly (Titus 2:13; Phil. 3:20; 1 Thess. 1:10). This hope is not running away. It is the strength to live a holy life today. Just as the apostles walked the road of martyrdom, the church has suffered for two thousand years, and that calling is the same whatever the timing.

The command not to receive the mark of the beast is the same for everyone, whatever the timing. We also firmly oppose the real dangers: setting dates (Matt. 24:36), teaching that a person must gain some special insight to be saved, and making money from the end times.

qa.q: 17. But if the pretribulation rapture is wrong, won't believers be caught unprepared and deceived?

a.p: No one will be deceived without knowing it at that time. The Antichrist will sit in the temple and claim to be God (2 Thess. 2:4), make war with the saints (Rev. 13:7), and keep anyone from buying or selling who does not receive a mark on the right hand or the forehead (Rev. 13:16–17). This is open persecution of those who believe in Jesus, so anyone will recognize it, and Scripture has already clearly warned that the mark must not be received (Rev. 14:9–11). If, without a rapture, a covenant for one week is confirmed (Dan. 9:27), the falling away takes place (2 Thess. 2:3), the abomination of desolation stands in the holy place (Matt. 24:15) and the judgments of Revelation begin, we will know right away: "So it was after the Tribulation." Both the pretribulation and the posttribulation views believe this order, so knowing it then will not be too late, and nothing will be lost. Whatever view we hold, if we come to stand in that place, there is only one thing to do: hold fast to Christ to the end (see Section 8, next).

sections.h: 8. What If a Figure Like the Antichrist Appears Without a Rapture?

body.p: "I believed in a pretribulation rapture. What if someone like the Antichrist appears and the rapture has not happened? What if we have already entered the Tribulation?" This is a question we must answer honestly. This section is not meant to cause fear. It is a guide, set out in advance from the Word, to help us discern and respond without being shaken when we hear such news.

body.h3: First: "Like the Antichrist" is not the same as "the Antichrist"

body.p: Already in the apostle John's day there were "many antichrists." Throughout church history, many rulers and public figures have been named as the Antichrist, and each time the naming missed the mark. The spirit that opposes God is at work in every age, so we do not conclude that someone is that final person just because such a figure appears. Scripture gives specific signs by which the final man of sin will be recognized.

ul: **A covenant** — he will confirm a covenant with many for one week (Dan. 9:27).
**Stopping the sacrifice** — in the middle of that week he will cause the sacrifice and the offering to cease (Dan. 9:27).
**Claiming to be God** — he will sit in the temple of God and present himself as God (2 Thess. 2:4; Matt. 24:15).
**Worship and the mark** — he will make people worship the image of the beast, and no one may buy or sell except those who have the mark (Rev. 13:15–17).

body.p: We do not look at one political leader, one technology or one system and say, "He has come." We look at whether these signs appear together, as the Word says.

body.h3: Second: In the pretribulation view, he is revealed after the church has left

body.p: In this view, the man of sin appears at the time when the restrainer is taken out of the way (2 Thess. 2:7–8; see ⑩ above). So to conclude that "the Antichrist has already come" while the church is still on earth actually does not fit this view. What we see now is most naturally read not as that final man himself, but as the work of "the mystery of iniquity" that prepares the way for him.

body.h3: Third: Scripture does not say that the rapture and the start of the seven years fall on the same day

body.p: What marks the start of the final seven years is not the rapture but the confirming of a covenant (Dan. 9:27). The rapture may happen at any time before that, but Scripture does not tell us how much time lies between the two. So if we hear news that holds out peace and safety, there is no reason to rush to the conclusion, "There was no rapture, so the pretribulation rapture was wrong." Scripture says that the time when such words are heard is all the more a time to stay awake.

body.h3: Fourth: Five things that will not be shaken, whatever comes first

ul: **Salvation does not depend on the timing of the rapture.** Our hope is not a timetable but Christ alone (Eph. 2:8; Heb. 13:8).

**The pretribulation rapture is not the belief that "Christians will not suffer."** When persecution comes, it does not mean that we have entered the seven years of wrath, and there is no reason for our faith to collapse (John 16:33; 1 Pet. 4:12).
**In no case will we worship the beast or receive its mark.** That mark comes together with a demand for worship, so those who know the Word can discern it (Rev. 14:9–10).
**We endure to the end and stay faithful unto death** (Matt. 24:13; Rev. 2:10; 12:11).

**We do not follow false christs or announced dates.** We do not follow those who say, "The Lord has already come to such-and-such a place," "Gather over here," or "Give up your property" (Matt. 24:23, 26).

body.h3: Fifth: When you hear such news — six steps

head: Step
What to do
Scripture
rows: **Check it against the Word.** Confirm it from the text of Scripture, not from videos, rumors or the news.
Acts 17:11
**Do not reach a conclusion alone.** Discern it together with the pastor of your church and your fellow believers.
1 John 4:1
**Keep up your daily life.** Do not abandon your work, studies or family. Staying faithful where you have been placed is what being awake looks like.
**Do not spread fear.** Do not pass on unconfirmed videos and posts. Comfort one another and build one another up.
1 Thess. 5:11
**Share the gospel.** Tell neighbors who are shaken that now is the time to turn to the Lord.
**Lift up your head and pray.**

body.h3: Sixth: If you have already been left behind

body.p: If you are reading this after the rapture has already happened, the door is not yet shut. Revelation shows a multitude that no one can number coming out of great tribulation. Turn to Christ now. Do not worship the beast, do not receive its mark, and endure to the end.

The pretribulation rapture is not "a plan to avoid suffering" but "the hope of waiting for the Bridegroom." We hold this hope on the basis of the Word. And whatever comes first, we pray that on the day the Lord comes for us, we will be standing as a bride who is awake.

qa.q: Can we know the date of the rapture?

a.p: No. Bible Insight opposes every attempt to set dates (see Section 10 below).

qa.q: Does this mean there are two Second Comings?

a.p: There is one Second Coming, and it takes place in two stages (see Objection 8 above). The coming in the air for His saints and the coming to the earth with His saints together make up one return.

qa.q: If there is still a chance after the rapture, is it all right not to believe now?

a.p: No. That the door of salvation is not shut after the rapture is news of grace, but it does not mean "I can believe later." Keeping the faith in the world left behind means paying a far greater price, even one's own life (Rev. 13:7; 20:4). The time Scripture speaks of is always today.

qa.q: Is "the mark of the beast" a vaccine or a chip in the body?

a.p: We do not identify any particular product or technology (vaccines, implanted chips, digital currency, cards and so on) as the mark of the beast. The mark in Revelation 13 is received by worshiping the beast and its image. It is a matter of a decision to abandon the faith (Rev. 14:9). It is not something a person receives without knowing it. For decisions about your health, please talk with medical professionals.

qa.q: Isn't talk about the end times a way of pushing faith on people through fear?

a.p: We do not mean to cause fear. After describing the rapture, Paul said, "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thess. 4:18), and right after speaking of the last days he said, "comfort yourselves together, and edify one another." This section leads not to despair but to hope.

qa.q: How should we treat churches and believers who hold another view?

a.p: We honor them as brothers and sisters waiting for the same Lord. It is enough to open the text together and talk humbly. We do not divide churches or condemn others over this question.

qa.q: What should we do today?

a.p: Watch and pray (Luke 21:36), live a holy life, purifying ourselves as He is pure (1 John 3:3), and share the gospel with neighbors who do not yet know Christ (2 Pet. 3:9). People with hope live today more faithfully.

body.p: Date-setting is teaching that names a particular day or year for the Second Coming or the rapture, and on account of that day leads people to give up their daily lives and their property. The "days" announced again and again in the last century all failed, and they left deep wounds in many families and churches.[^24] We clearly oppose the following teachings.

ul: Teaching that sets a date and announces the Second Coming or the rapture
Teaching that tells people to leave their work, studies or families because of that day
Teaching that tells people to give away their property because of that day
Teaching that claims "direct revelation" in order to make people follow a particular leader

body.p: This section also does not interpret today's international affairs, wars or any particular nation as the fulfillment of prophecy, and it does not name any real person as the Antichrist.

Though our views differ, what we confess together is the same: that Jesus will come again as He promised, that the dead will rise again, and that God will make all things new. And that salvation comes through Christ alone (John 14:6; Acts 4:12). As the old saying of the church puts it: in essentials, unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity.[^25]

After describing the rapture, Paul ends with these words: "Wherefore comfort one another with these words" (1 Thess. 4:18). The purpose of the rapture doctrine is not argument but comfort: the comfort of meeting again the believers who have fallen asleep before us, the comfort of being appointed not to wrath but to salvation, and above all the comfort that "so shall we ever be with the Lord." Our views may differ, but we are waiting for the same Bridegroom.
Until the day He comes again, let us keep watch and walk together. Maranatha.
